segments.title: If Jellicoe had turned towards the torpedoes at Jutland
segments.body: Turning towards the torpedoes at Jutland could have cost Jellicoe about a third of his capital ships or more. The estimate is speculative and depends on how many ships were hit. It also depends on how well their underwater protection contained the damage. The outcome of the battle is left open.

evidence.note: A counterfactual about British capital-ship losses turns on the number of hits and how well the ships withstand them.

segments.summary: A counterfactual about British capital-ship losses turns on the number of hits and how well the ships withstand them.
segments.question: How many capital ships might Jellicoe have lost if he had turned towards the torpedoes at Jutland, and what would that have meant for the battle?
segments.answerShort: The estimate is about a third of the capital ships or potentially more. The estimate depends on how many ships were hit and how well their underwater protection held.

segments.title: Anime mascots and military recruiting in Japan
segments.body: Japan's military uses anime mascots. Financial support for military-themed games and anime comes up as another way to reach recruits. Azur Lane is one of the examples raised. The approach is judged effective in Japan. Its reception in other countries is left open.

evidence.note: Japan's military mascots prompt a question about whether other countries could use anime and games to reach recruits.

segments.summary: Japan's military mascots prompt a question about whether other countries could use anime and games to reach recruits.
segments.question: Do Japan's armed forces use anime mascots and games to help recruit, and could the same approach work elsewhere?
segments.answerShort: The approach is judged effective in Japan. How well it would work elsewhere remains open.

segments.title: Designing an all-calibres battleship in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The game build starts with the largest guns, including 20-inch, 19-inch and 18-inch weapons. The hull needs more beam as the mounts go on, and the design speed comes down to 28 knots. Triple turrets are selected for the largest guns to get more use out of the available space. Carrying all these calibres on one hull is the audience's design brief.

evidence.note: An audience challenge to fit every available calibre onto a Soviet hull puts beam, speed and turret arrangement in competition.

segments.summary: An audience challenge to fit every available calibre onto a Soviet hull puts beam, speed and turret arrangement in competition.

segments.title: Fitting the turrets and controlling their fire
segments.body: Fire control is already a concern while the smaller weapons are still going aboard. Turning off automatic duplication allows turrets to be placed individually where there is room. Single mounts are used for some calibres as the design moves down from the largest guns to the secondaries. Finding deck space still leaves the problem of coordinating fire from the mixed battery.

evidence.note: The all-calibres game battleship has a crowded deck plan and a battery expected to be difficult to control.

segments.summary: The all-calibres game battleship has a crowded deck plan and a battery expected to be difficult to control.

segments.title: What the all-calibres battleship must carry
segments.body: The challenge calls for a gun of every available calibre on a single hull. Several smaller mounts go on quickly. Finding space for the 8-inch gun takes longer, and it finally goes on near the end of the exchange. The design uses a Soviet hull.

evidence.note: The audience asks about the game build's objective just as the remaining calibres become difficult to fit.

segments.summary: The audience asks about the game build's objective just as the remaining calibres become difficult to fit.
segments.question: What is the all-calibres battleship supposed to carry?
segments.answerShort: The game challenge is to fit at least one gun of every available calibre on a single battleship hull.

segments.title: Gun placement, stability and engine efficiency
segments.body: The suggested positions would make room for more armament. The game's stability and engine-efficiency readouts give reasons to avoid them. The ship already has stability problems, so the extra mounting space comes at a cost.

evidence.note: A suggestion to use spaces around the funnel or at the ends of the ship exposes the compromises in a crowded battleship design.

segments.summary: A suggestion to use spaces around the funnel or at the ends of the ship exposes the compromises in a crowded battleship design.
segments.question: Why avoid placing guns near the funnels or at the ends of the all-calibres game battleship?
segments.answerShort: The proposed positions affect the game's stability and engine-efficiency ratings on a ship whose stability is already a concern.

segments.title: Keeping the all-calibres battleship usable in the game
segments.body: Ranging equipment and radio go aboard as the design shifts from armament to support systems. The game's veteran crew setting is considered important with so many calibres to manage. The design also gets the maximum bulkhead setting, a double hull and torpedo protection. These choices give the experimental design a chance once it leaves the ship designer.

evidence.note: After the guns go aboard, the design adds ranging equipment, radio and protection for a ship expected to be hard to fight.

segments.summary: After the guns go aboard, the design adds ranging equipment, radio and protection for a ship expected to be hard to fight.

segments.title: Speed and space in a simulated British battleship
segments.body: Even a hull described as displacing 112,000 tons runs up against the designer's limits. Lowering the speed setting creates space and going lower opens up further options for range and equipment. Spacious crew accommodation also claims some of that allowance. A proposed 16.5-inch gun fit gives way to further trials when it proves difficult to place on the hull.

evidence.note: Reducing the speed requirement opens room for armament and crew accommodations in the Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts designer.

segments.summary: Reducing the speed requirement opens room for armament and crew accommodations in the Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts designer.

segments.title: A Town-class cruiser's worth of guns on each side
segments.body: Six-inch secondary guns give the vessel something like a Town-class cruiser's battery on each side. Quintuple torpedo mounts add another weapons system. The shell and loading choices differ between the main battery and the secondary guns. The cruiser comparison conveys how much armament the proposed battleship carries besides its main guns.

evidence.note: A British game battleship carries a secondary battery compared to a Town-class cruiser's armament on either beam.

segments.summary: A British game battleship carries a secondary battery compared to a Town-class cruiser's armament on either beam.

segments.title: Armour, pitch and trim on the simulated Duncan
segments.body: The design work turns from weapons to the main deck, belt armour and stability. Reducing pitch and roll is meant to give the guns a steadier platform. Changes to the main belt and fore-and-aft weight bring the hull closer to balance. Some stern-heavy trim remains when the design is renamed Duncan.

evidence.note: The British design is adjusted for steadier gunnery while its armour and fore-and-aft balance are still being worked out.

segments.summary: The British design is adjusted for steadier gunnery while its armour and fore-and-aft balance are still being worked out.

segments.title: Radar and ranging with a mixed-calibre battery
segments.body: Before launch, the Soviet design gets a check of its auxiliary machinery and stability. A steadier ship gives the unusual battery a better chance of working. Once the ships are in action, radar appears to help. Finding the range for shots from so many different weapons remains a problem.

evidence.note: Radar and better stability help the Soviet ship in the game, where its many different weapons complicate ranging.

segments.summary: Radar and better stability help the Soviet ship in the game, where its many different weapons complicate ranging.

segments.title: Scaling a King George V design to 18-inch guns
segments.body: Duncan is described as an enlarged adaptation of a twelve-gun King George V scheme. The model takes that layout up to 18-inch guns. As hits become scarce on the opposing ship, attention returns to the effort to give it a stable platform. The game trial puts this concentrated British main battery up against the Soviet all-calibre exercise.

evidence.note: A twelve-gun King George V scheme supplies the starting point for the British game ship Duncan.

segments.summary: A twelve-gun King George V scheme supplies the starting point for the British game ship Duncan.

segments.title: A technically viable oddity in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The example is described as technically viable even though it is unusual. The assessment focuses on whether the design was suited to its role. The details of the ship's configuration are difficult to make out.

evidence.note: Viewer asks about unusual viable creations. The ship name and configuration are unclear.

segments.summary: An unusual game build stands out because it was judged capable of doing the job it was designed for.
segments.question: Which Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts build stands out as particularly unusual?
segments.answerShort: One unusual build is singled out because it remained technically viable and suited its role.

segments.title: British awareness of Japan's Number 13 class
segments.body: The exchange concerns the prospective Number 13 class. British knowledge is described in broad terms. The extent of that knowledge remains open.

evidence.note: Britain is said to have had some awareness of the Japanese battleship plans.

segments.summary: Britain is said to have had some awareness of the Japanese battleship plans.
segments.question: Did Britain know about Japan's Number 13 class?
segments.answerShort: Yes in broad terms. Britain had some idea of what Japan was planning.

segments.title: Why battlecruisers could struggle to stay in a battle line
segments.body: Battlecruisers could start in line, but their protection depended in part on speed and sharp manoeuvres. An armoured battleship could hold a steadier course and rely more heavily on its protection. A battleship trying to follow a faster manoeuvre could compromise its own gunnery. A battlecruiser obliged to keep to the battleship's profile gave up some of the movement on which its survival depended.

evidence.note: Speed and freedom to manoeuvre help explain why a line of battlecruisers could break up once the fighting started.

segments.summary: Speed and freedom to manoeuvre help explain why a line of battlecruisers could break up once the fighting started.
segments.question: Would battlecruisers use the same line-of-battle tactics as battleships when fighting other battlecruisers?
segments.answerShort: They could form a line. The need to keep speed up and manoeuvre freely could soon break that formation.

segments.title: Can a 40-knot battlecruiser carry 15-inch guns and armour?
segments.body: The brief calls for 40 knots, guns of at least 15 inches and some armour. Hull shape, machinery and protection all have to fit the game's displacement allowance. The completed design concentrates twelve 15-inch guns forward and has a stated cruising speed of 33 knots. A heavy cruiser is chosen for the trial as the sort of ship a lone battlecruiser might hunt.

evidence.note: The game challenge produces a long, slim battlecruiser with all twelve main guns forward for a trial against a heavy cruiser.

segments.summary: The game challenge produces a long, slim battlecruiser with all twelve main guns forward for a trial against a heavy cruiser.
segments.question: Can you build a 40-knot battlecruiser with 15-inch guns and some armour?
segments.answerShort: The simulator allows a 40-knot design with twelve 15-inch guns and some armour after changes to hull dimensions, propulsion and weight.

segments.title: Hull and machinery for a 40-knot game battlecruiser
segments.body: A heavy cruiser is chosen as the opponent before work begins on the hull. Several hulls look plausible in the designer, and the selected one needs a little more beam. Restricted space rules out some of the fittings. A funnel and enough range to satisfy the brief still have to fit before the 15-inch guns are laid out.

evidence.note: The requested speed drives the choice of hull, beam and the machinery fittings that will fit aboard.

segments.summary: The requested speed drives the choice of hull, beam and the machinery fittings that will fit aboard.

segments.title: Paying for 40 knots in armour and displacement
segments.body: The design starts with an ambitious layout and pares it back against the game's limits. A twelve-gun battery sets the baseline, while hull protection and bulkheads offer places to change the weight bill. The machinery gets the ship to 40 knots in the game, where the hull is already overweight before the armour adjustments. Cutting armour brings it within the limit and makes room for secondary guns.

evidence.note: Once the speed and main battery are set, hull protection has to fit the remaining weight.

segments.summary: Once the speed and main battery are set, hull protection has to fit the remaining weight.

segments.title: Radar, secondary guns and exposed armour on the 40-knot design
segments.body: Twin secondary mounts add weight to a design already close to its limit. Radar is kept even when the ship comes out roughly 500 tons overweight. Protection is reduced selectively, with more armour retained where the design is expected to draw fire. That helps bring the ship back within its allowance.

evidence.note: The last weight cuts preserve radar and concentrate armour on the parts expected to be exposed to fire.

segments.summary: The last weight cuts preserve radar and concentrate armour on the parts expected to be exposed to fire.

segments.title: Twelve guns forward on the simulated battlecruiser
segments.body: The ship is long and slim, with a stated cruising speed of 33 knots in the game. Its twelve 15-inch guns sit forward. That arrangement is explained in terms of fore-and-aft weight balance. The battlecruiser withstands a torpedo hit in the simulated engagement with the heavy cruiser.

evidence.note: The finished hull puts the main battery forward to balance its weight and takes a torpedo hit during the trial.

segments.summary: The finished hull puts the main battery forward to balance its weight and takes a torpedo hit during the trial.

segments.title: Optically guided weapons versus heavy naval guns
segments.body: Optically guided weapons against ships had been considered. The answer puts usable guidance within the range of existing heavy guns. If both weapons could reach the same target, a heavy gun was judged the more efficient choice in that engagement.

evidence.note: Heavy guns are the point of comparison when considering an optically guided ship-to-ship weapon with limited reach.

segments.summary: Heavy guns are the point of comparison when considering an optically guided ship-to-ship weapon with limited reach.
segments.question: Were optically guided ship-to-ship weapons contemplated, and were they practical?
segments.answerShort: They were contemplated. At the ranges envisaged, heavy naval guns could already engage the target more efficiently.

segments.title: A post-1920 ship with its firepower on the beams
segments.body: The brief allows any nation and calls for post-1920 design assumptions. Most of the firepower is meant to face out from rows along the sides, with limited arcs. The game ship masses 6-inch guns for broadside fire and has to turn beam-on in its trial. A later look back judges that it captured the broadside idea while missing part of the brief.

evidence.note: Brief for a post-1920 ship carrying most of its weapons in outward-facing rows.
The six-inch battery fires in the game trial as the ship turns beam-on.
The original brief is restated and the completed build is judged a partial match.

segments.summary: A game build translates rows of outward-facing guns into a broadside cruiser with restricted firing arcs.
segments.question: Can you build a post-1920 ship carrying most of its firepower in outward-facing rows along its sides?
segments.answerShort: The game produces a cruiser with rows of 6-inch guns for fighting beam-on. It only partially matches the brief.

segments.title: Fitting a broadside battery into a 20,000-ton cruiser
segments.body: The cruiser is described at about 20,000 tons. Even the smaller guns can have wider arcs than intended, so their coverage is reduced. Triple torpedo mounts add weight as the ship goes several hundred tons over its limit. Reducing hull protection recovers part of the difference, leaving more cuts to make before the test.

evidence.note: The broadside design narrows gun arcs and trades hull protection against the weight of additional weapons.

segments.summary: The broadside design narrows gun arcs and trades hull protection against the weight of additional weapons.

segments.title: A massed 6-inch broadside against heavier guns
segments.body: The broadside ship has to turn beam-on to bring its rows of guns to bear. The volume of 6-inch fire prompts a distinction between armour surviving an initial strike and enduring repeated impacts. The simulated ship carries the lighter battery on a heavy-cruiser-sized hull. The fight is close enough for a mutual loss to look plausible before it ends.

evidence.note: A game cruiser has to expose its side to use the full weight of its lighter guns against a heavy cruiser.

segments.summary: A game cruiser has to expose its side to use the full weight of its lighter guns against a heavy cruiser.

segments.title: What holding Singapore would have required in World War II
segments.body: An armoured division and at least one more infantry division are proposed to counter Japanese manoeuvre in Malaya. The fleet would have had at least four carriers and four capital ships, backed by escorts, submarines and supply ships. The local air force would probably have needed to be trebled. Even if that concentration made defence possible, assigning those resources to Singapore would have left other fronts short.

evidence.note: A counterfactual weighs the land, air and naval reinforcements needed in Malaya against the demands of other fronts.

segments.summary: A counterfactual weighs the land, air and naval reinforcements needed in Malaya against the demands of other fronts.
segments.question: What would it have taken to hold Singapore during World War II?
segments.answerShort: Major land and air reinforcements and a large, supported fleet would have been needed at the cost of forces on other fronts.

segments.title: A battleship with battlecruiser armour
segments.body: The build keeps a 6-inch belt, and the simulator still allows heavier deck protection. The Russian cruiser starts astern in fog and soon faces twelve 18-inch guns. The account puts the outcome down to roughly three hits. The brief trial shows what the heavy guns can do against a cruiser and leaves the battleship's own protection largely untested.

evidence.note: A viewer's design challenge puts a lightly protected battleship with twelve 18-inch guns against a Russian heavy cruiser in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts.

segments.summary: A viewer's design challenge puts a lightly protected battleship with twelve 18-inch guns against a Russian heavy cruiser in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts.
segments.question: How would a battleship with battlecruiser-style armour fare against a heavy cruiser in the game?
segments.answerShort: The design carries a 6-inch belt, and its twelve 18-inch guns quickly overwhelm the cruiser.

segments.title: A proposed Tribal-class destroyer successor
segments.body: The game design takes shape around a 1938 fit with torpedoes and 4.5-inch guns. A 40-calibre barrel is preferred for the 4.5-inch gun, and the simulator offers a shorter weapon. The design speed comes down to 36 knots. The available curved towers are judged unlike Royal Navy practice of the period. The design is called Trafalgar and still has stability problems.

evidence.note: A 1938-era design in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts explores what a successor to the Royal Navy's Tribal class could carry.

segments.summary: A 1938-era design in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts explores what a successor to the Royal Navy's Tribal class could carry.

segments.title: Royal Navy torpedo options beyond the standard calibre
segments.body: The fit in the game prompts a distinction between a standard weapon and a development option. The reply points to British work on a larger calibre that would have been available in principle. It treats that weapon as an option the Royal Navy had yet to pursue. The mention of a 23-inch setting in the game leaves the historical designation and associated class uncertain.

evidence.note: A viewer challenges the 23-inch torpedo fit on the simulated destroyer.

segments.summary: A viewer challenges the 23-inch torpedo fit on the simulated destroyer.
segments.question: Why use a nonstandard torpedo calibre on the British destroyer design?
segments.answerShort: British development work is cited as the basis for treating a larger calibre as a possible option.

segments.title: Pitch and weight distribution on a destroyer design
segments.body: Moving a component aft only slightly improves pitch, and later adjustments make the game's pitch figure worse. Roll and foreweight offset can move independently of pitch. One bridge arrangement hangs over the forward torpedoes. The designer has reached the largest available hull by the time the ship goes to trial. Ballast comes up as a real-world correction that the simulator struggles to represent.

evidence.note: The proposed Tribal successor exposes the limits of moving weapons, changing bridge structures and expanding hull size to correct pitch in the simulator.

segments.summary: The proposed Tribal successor exposes the limits of moving weapons, changing bridge structures and expanding hull size to correct pitch in the simulator.

segments.title: A destroyer duel against a cruiser-like opponent
segments.body: The game's Russian opponent looks more like a light cruiser, with triple 5.1-inch gun mounts. The destroyer tries to reach torpedo range and uses smoke and changes of course to stay in the fight. It loses the duel. Several destroyers were expected to work together, a condition absent from the trial.

evidence.note: A one-on-one test of the proposed Tribal successor illustrates the difference between fighting alone and operating as part of a flotilla.

segments.summary: A one-on-one test of the proposed Tribal successor illustrates the difference between fighting alone and operating as part of a flotilla.

segments.title: Soviet destroyer size and small formations
segments.body: One explanation links the size of Soviet destroyers to the number of ships expected to be available for a fight. With fewer ships, the assumption was that they would be more likely to operate singly or in pairs. That in turn favoured more capability on each hull.

evidence.note: A comparison with the simulator's large destroyers raises a historical explanation for Soviet interest in bigger ships.

segments.summary: A comparison with the simulator's large destroyers raises a historical explanation for Soviet interest in bigger ships.

segments.title: A destroyer hull with light-cruiser firepower
segments.body: The game allows a destroyer hull to carry several triple turrets and a torpedo launcher. The gun layout and overall firepower make the vessel look closer to a light cruiser. It survives its encounter while the opposing cruiser is lost. The game describes the ship by hull type even when its battery resembles that of a different class of warship.

evidence.note: A computer-designed Soviet-style ship in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts blurs the category line between a destroyer and a light cruiser.

segments.summary: A computer-designed Soviet-style ship in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts blurs the category line between a destroyer and a light cruiser.

segments.title: An interwar coastal defence ship for Norway
segments.body: The choice begins between a cruiser and a small battleship, then moves to a heavy-cruiser hull in the game's 1925 setting. A compact ship with limited speed and short operating range is the starting point. Heavy guns go forward, with lighter secondary and anti-aircraft weapons. Attempts to control pitch and roll push the hull wider and deeper, making the ship heavier and forcing further adjustments.

evidence.note: A viewer's counterfactual asks what Britain could build for Norwegian coastal defence against a future German attack.

segments.summary: A viewer's counterfactual asks what Britain could build for Norwegian coastal defence against a future German attack.
segments.question: What kind of interwar British-built ship could help Norway defend its coast against a German attack?
segments.answerShort: The simulated design uses a 1925 heavy-cruiser hull for a compact coastal defender with heavy guns forward. Stability and weight become the main constraints.

segments.title: Speed, range and period equipment for a coastal defender
segments.body: The early design calls for a compact hull at the lowest practical weight. Coastal service motivates limiting range, and the first speed target is 20 knots. As the hull and machinery change, 24 knots is described as unexpectedly fast for the concept. The build uses radar available in the game, an acknowledged anachronism for the simulated year of 1925.

evidence.note: The simulated Norwegian coastal defence ship starts with a 20-knot target and limited range.

segments.summary: The simulated Norwegian coastal defence ship starts with a 20-knot target and limited range.

segments.title: Forward heavy guns and lighter batteries
segments.body: The heavy battery goes forward to make the compact design work. The proposed 6-inch secondaries give way to 5.5-inch guns, treated as a viable period calibre for the role. Three-inch weapons are added for anti-aircraft defence.

evidence.note: A hypothetical Norwegian ship concentrates its heavy guns forward and uses period British calibres for secondary and anti-aircraft duties.

segments.summary: A hypothetical Norwegian ship concentrates its heavy guns forward and uses period British calibres for secondary and anti-aircraft duties.

segments.title: Hull width, draught and weight on a coastal defence ship
segments.body: After the gun layout is settled, the design still shows troublesome pitch and roll. More beam helps the game's stability readout at the cost of a heavier hull. Increasing draught puts further pressure on displacement. The design is reported to be 430 tons overweight before more adjustments.

evidence.note: Stability problems on the simulated Norwegian design lead to a wider, deeper hull and a displacement overrun.

segments.summary: Stability problems on the simulated Norwegian design lead to a wider, deeper hull and a displacement overrun.

segments.title: Armour and torpedoes in the Norwegian design trial
segments.body: The cruiser brings six 9.7-inch guns in the game, with an unusually large torpedo load. The Norwegian design aims to stay outside the cruiser's torpedo reach. Its belt armour absorbs hits while the cruiser suffers damage and fires. Armour and range both influence this particular simulation.

evidence.note: A simulated Norwegian capital ship meets a heavy cruiser that relies heavily on torpedoes.

segments.summary: A simulated Norwegian capital ship meets a heavy cruiser that relies heavily on torpedoes.

segments.title: The case for a South Korean aircraft carrier
segments.body: A carrier is a plausible option given the importance of South Korea's sea lines of communication. The need to defend them gives the proposal a purpose. The broader strategic case for committing to a carrier remains unsettled.

evidence.note: South Korea's maritime communications give it a reason to consider a carrier.

segments.summary: South Korea's maritime communications give it a reason to consider a carrier.
segments.question: Should South Korea pursue an aircraft carrier?
segments.answerShort: Sea lines of communication give South Korea a reason to consider one. The full strategic case remains open.

segments.title: Compact cruise missiles and shipboard strike capacity
segments.body: The proposal is to carry more compact cruise missiles and make strike capacity more affordable. Related options have been explored, with viability depending on the capability they buy for the price. Railguns and advanced guns come up as other areas of development. The failure of the Advanced Gun System is attributed mainly to poor control of the programme's scope.

evidence.note: Compact cruise missile proposal, cost and capability comparison, and the criticism of AGS programme scope.

segments.summary: A question about getting more strike rounds for the money leads to a programme lesson from the Advanced Gun System.
segments.question: Could a compact, low-cost cruise missile increase shipboard strike capacity?
segments.answerShort: The idea depends on how much capability it buys for the money. The Advanced Gun System is cited as a warning about programme scope.

segments.title: Why France completed Jean Bart
segments.body: Completing Jean Bart gave France a public symbol of recovery. In this account, great-power standing mattered when other naval units also competed for resources. This puts the politics of commissioning the battleship alongside the question of what the fleet needed.

evidence.note: The battleship's completion gave France a visible sign of postwar recovery and great-power standing.

segments.summary: The battleship's completion gave France a visible sign of postwar recovery and great-power standing.
segments.question: Why did France complete Jean Bart when it could have put resources into other warships?
segments.answerShort: The battleship symbolised postwar reconstruction and France's standing as a great power.

segments.title: Larger command ships and uncrewed vessels in European fleets
segments.body: The forecast covers larger European navies as well as smaller ones. Crewed warships could grow as they take on command of groups of uncrewed vessels, which could fill some of the smaller roles and add numbers to the fleet. Even the smaller vessels could reach roughly 2,000 to 3,000 tonnes in this forecast. A radar picket is one example of a ship that could need room for fuel, electronics and backup systems.

evidence.note: One forecast has European navies adding hulls by mixing larger crewed command ships with uncrewed vessels.

segments.summary: One forecast has European navies adding hulls by mixing larger crewed command ships with uncrewed vessels.
segments.question: Will smaller European navies end up with fewer, bigger ships or more small ships?
segments.answerShort: The forecast has larger crewed command ships and more numerous uncrewed vessels in some of the smaller roles.

segments.title: Why uncrewed ships need more redundancy
segments.body: A crew can repair a failed system while another unit keeps the ship operating. An uncrewed vessel has to wait for maintenance to reach it and may need more spares or parallel systems. The example is a ship that needs two functioning positioning systems and has to carry extra units to cover failures. Those backups take up space even on a ship with a specialised role such as a radar picket.

evidence.note: Navigation equipment illustrates how the absence of onboard repair crews affects the systems an uncrewed ship has to carry.

segments.summary: Navigation equipment illustrates how the absence of onboard repair crews affects the systems an uncrewed ship has to carry.

segments.title: Which design followed the wartime Tribals in the game?
segments.body: The request concerns a follow-on to the Tribal-class destroyers. The reply points back to the proposed successor already built and tested earlier in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts. Its simulated encounter with a Soviet cruiser identifies which trial to watch.

evidence.note: The answer points back to the simulated destroyer fight with a Soviet cruiser.
Earlier trial of the proposed Tribal successor against a Russian opponent.

segments.summary: The question returns to a design exercise that ended in a duel with a Soviet cruiser.
segments.question: Has the follow-on design for the Tribal-class destroyers already been tried?
segments.answerShort: Yes. The answer points back to the simulated trial against a Soviet cruiser.

segments.title: Designing a 1930s cruiser for the fictional Albonian Navy
segments.body: The Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts build answers a request for an interwar cruiser that looks good on paper and performs poorly. It combines components modelled on ships from different navies and takes cues from the German Panzerschiff. The model is stable even with very little protection on deck. Its poor gunnery leads to a criticism of split main batteries and the difficulties of controlling their fire.

evidence.note: A viewer asks for a cruiser with impressive specifications that conceal serious weaknesses.

segments.summary: A viewer asks for a cruiser with impressive specifications that conceal serious weaknesses.
segments.question: How would you design a 1930s cruiser for the fictional Albonian Navy that looks good on paper and performs poorly?
segments.answerShort: The game build takes cues from the Panzerschiff and looks stable in the designer. It sacrifices deck protection and has gunnery problems in the trial.

segments.title: Mixing British and Japanese components on the Albonian cruiser
segments.body: A British forward section is paired with a Japanese component. Their fit is awkward even on the design screen. The game allows combinations that could not readily be built. A later readout puts simulated engine efficiency at about 53 percent, another sign that the assembled profile conceals performance problems.

evidence.note: The fictional design combines components that would be impractical to fit together on a real ship.

segments.summary: The fictional design combines components that would be impractical to fit together on a real ship.

segments.title: A stable cruiser with no deck armour
segments.body: The ship starts this portion overweight. Stability is deliberately kept respectable so the specification looks credible. The deck has no armour, even with the guns and torpedoes set for the game trial. The favourable stability rating says little about the quality of the protection scheme.

evidence.note: The fictional cruiser meets a visible design goal while leaving a gap in protection.

segments.summary: The fictional cruiser meets a visible design goal while leaving a gap in protection.

segments.title: The Albonian cruiser's guns in action
segments.body: The cruiser does little damage at its initial range and closes in the simulation. The 3-inch guns seem to be the most accurate weapons once they can fire. The simulated exchange shows how a seemingly powerful main battery can accomplish little when the heavy guns struggle to hit.

evidence.note: Much of the useful fire in the fictional cruiser's trial comes from its 3-inch guns.

segments.summary: Much of the useful fire in the fictional cruiser's trial comes from its 3-inch guns.

segments.title: A split main battery as a fire-control problem
segments.body: The discussion turns from the simulation to the practice of splitting a warship's main battery between opposite ends of the hull. The criticism is that this can complicate fire control and reduce what the ship achieves with the guns it carries. It is offered as a reason to assess the layout beyond its paper specifications.

evidence.note: The Albonian trial prompts a criticism of the Panzerschiff's gun layout.

segments.summary: The Albonian trial prompts a criticism of the Panzerschiff's gun layout.

segments.title: How large might a hypothetical North Korean cruiser be?
segments.body: A small light cruiser provides the rough size benchmark for the imagined North Korean ship. The estimate is off the cuff. Its armour scheme is left open.

evidence.note: A small light cruiser is offered as a rough size comparison.

segments.summary: A small light cruiser is offered as a rough size comparison.
segments.question: What size and armour might a hypothetical North Korean cruiser have?
segments.answerShort: The suggested benchmark is a small light cruiser. The armour is left unspecified.

segments.title: Fitting an A, B and Q turret layout to the G3
segments.body: The A, B and Q arrangement can be assembled in the game. A component intended for the G3 fails to fit where expected, and the permitted positioning takes the arrangement farther aft than desired. The resulting layout approximates the proposal within the game's restrictions.

evidence.note: The G3 pattern runs into the ship designer's rules about placement in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts.

segments.summary: The G3 pattern runs into the ship designer's rules about placement in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts.
segments.question: Can the G3's A, B and Q turret pattern be reproduced in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts?
segments.answerShort: Yes, in approximate form. The game makes some components sit farther aft than intended.

segments.title: Starting a design with maximum survivability
segments.body: The game build starts by selecting the highest survivability settings. The idea is to lower them as needed to fit the ship. The same process is compared to a procurement project that starts with the protection its designers want and is revised into a version that can be afforded.

evidence.note: A comparison with real procurement explains why a game build can start with the best protection settings and then cut them back.

segments.summary: A comparison with real procurement explains why a game build can start with the best protection settings and then cut them back.

segments.title: Fitting funnels and reducing weight on the G3 model
segments.body: The available funnels will not fit on the original superstructure. A smaller funnel option leaves a second to place, so the superstructure has to change. The model then comes down to its displacement limit at the chosen speed setting. Pitch and secondary armament still need work when that weight target is met.

evidence.note: The G3 needs a different superstructure to fit its funnels and still has to reach the intended displacement.

segments.summary: The G3 needs a different superstructure to fit its funnels and still has to reach the intended displacement.

segments.title: Why armour substitutes for ballast in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The stock designer has no independent ballast adjustment. Thickening the belt and deck can satisfy its balance calculation, so the armour reflects the simulator's rules as well as the intended protection. Another constraint appears when none of the available funnels fit the large secondary tower. The stock game provides a common set of rules and parts for these challenges.

evidence.note: A G3-inspired battlecruiser exposes a limit of the stock game's stability model when armour doubles as ballast.

segments.summary: A G3-inspired battlecruiser exposes a limit of the stock game's stability model when armour doubles as ballast.

segments.title: Gun blast and clear firing arcs
segments.body: The game allows the battlecruiser to fire across its own superstructure. Aboard a real ship, muzzle blast can damage nearby structure. The available firing arc depends on the turret and what lies around it. Even when a turret can train onto a target, the ship's heading may have to change to give the guns clearance.

evidence.note: A simulated broadside illustrates the difference between the direction a turret can point and the arc in which it can safely fire.

segments.summary: A simulated broadside illustrates the difference between the direction a turret can point and the arc in which it can safely fire.

segments.title: A postwar Tribal-class destroyer in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The custom battle designer supplies a large hull for an imagined descendant of the 1936 Tribal class. Its shape draws an unfavourable comparison with the British Daring class. The build tries several gun sizes on a crowded deck and selects oil-fired gas turbines. Changing dimensions and range affects the simulated ship's handling and displacement, with pitch remaining a problem.

evidence.note: A viewer requests a 1960s successor to the wartime Tribal class. The game build tests the proposed weapons against deck space, weight and pitch.

segments.summary: A viewer requests a 1960s successor to the wartime Tribal class. The game build tests the proposed weapons against deck space, weight and pitch.
segments.question: What would a postwar version of the Second World War Tribal-class destroyer look like?
segments.answerShort: The game build uses a large 1960s destroyer hull with mixed-calibre guns and gas turbines. Crowded mount positions, excess weight and persistent pitch constrain the result.

segments.title: Deck space limits the postwar Tribal variant
segments.body: A position that looks too wide for one mount is kept for a half-inch gun. The design also calls for 3-inch and 40 mm weapons, and the hull leaves little room for the requested 40 mm mounts. The list of weapons already has to be reconsidered before the ship reaches its displacement check.

evidence.note: The proposed Tribal successor runs short of useful places to put its smaller gun mounts.

segments.summary: The proposed Tribal successor runs short of useful places to put its smaller gun mounts.

segments.title: Beam, displacement and pitch on the Tribal variant
segments.body: The simulated destroyer starts well over its weight allowance. The stated speed drops to 36 knots and the design switches to gas turbines. Roll becomes more manageable while the game still reports persistent pitch, including a 65 percent readout during one adjustment. A change to beam improves the pitch estimate and the design goes over its weight limit again.

evidence.note: The game designer shows what changing speed, range and hull dimensions does to the destroyer's weight and pitch.

segments.summary: The game designer shows what changing speed, range and hull dimensions does to the destroyer's weight and pitch.

segments.title: What if a German Panzerschiff carried four 14-inch guns?
segments.body: A German Panzerschiff with 14-inch guns would make an immediate impression abroad. Four barrels could mean taking longer to establish a firing solution. Depending on when the change happened, it could also put pressure on the treaty system's 14-inch standard. In that scenario, the King George V class might carry nine 16-inch guns, and Nelson and Rodney might receive refits.

evidence.note: Reaction to the twins in place of triples and the problem of ranging with four guns.
Later discussion of the 14-inch treaty standard, King George V, Nelson and Rodney.

segments.summary: A counterfactual replaces triple 11-inch turrets with twin 14-inch mounts, raising questions about spotting salvos and the naval treaties.
segments.question: How might other navies respond if a German Panzerschiff used twin 14-inch turrets in place of triple 11-inch turrets?
segments.answerShort: The larger calibre would attract attention, although the low barrel count could slow ranging. Depending on the timing, the change might also reopen treaty negotiations and alter British battleship plans.

segments.title: How Project Habakkuk might have changed Cold War carrier strategy
segments.body: The counterfactual turns on whether a pykrete platform could work across a useful range of latitudes. Its size invites thought experiments about operating aircraft such as the SR-71 Blackbird and Avro Vulcan, which would require much more runway than ordinary carrier aircraft. An ocean-going airfield of that size might have changed the case for conventional supercarriers. The proposal also raises questions about how to power, repair and crew such a ship.

evidence.note: A viewer asks what a completed pykrete carrier could have meant for naval aviation if it operated as a floating airfield.

segments.summary: A viewer asks what a completed pykrete carrier could have meant for naval aviation if it operated as a floating airfield.
segments.question: How could a completed Project Habakkuk ice carrier have changed Cold War naval strategy?
segments.answerShort: If a pykrete vessel could operate across latitudes, it might serve as a mobile air base for unusually large aircraft and change how navies invested in carriers.

segments.title: Nuclear electric propulsion for a Habakkuk-scale carrier
segments.body: One option is a nuclear plant supplying electricity to multiple propulsion drives. Distributing power on that scale leads to the idea of early integrated electric propulsion. A successful example might have encouraged navies to consider nuclear propulsion for other carriers. This is a possible postwar development in the counterfactual.

evidence.note: An imagined Cold War Habakkuk raises the question of how to power a vessel the size of a floating island.

segments.summary: An imagined Cold War Habakkuk raises the question of how to power a vessel the size of a floating island.

segments.title: How a floating Habakkuk base might stay in service
segments.body: The suggested service life depends on renewing the hull and upgrading its systems. A platform of that size would have to undergo much of this work without normal dry-dock access. It could carry supplies and troops and have an internal dock for smaller vessels. If the repairs were practical, a treasury might see the appeal of one large initial investment followed by upgrades.

evidence.note: A pykrete carrier's size opens up room for an internal dock while making conventional dry-dock maintenance difficult.

segments.summary: A pykrete carrier's size opens up room for an internal dock while making conventional dry-dock maintenance difficult.

segments.title: Airfield layout and crew demands on Habakkuk
segments.body: A vessel of this size could put a missile installation well away from the runway. That separation would be hard to achieve on a conventional flight deck. The imagined scale runs to miles in some versions of the thought experiment. The space for extra facilities comes with a substantial crewing burden.

evidence.note: An enlarged Habakkuk might have room to separate aviation and missile facilities at the cost of a much larger crew.

segments.summary: An enlarged Habakkuk might have room to separate aviation and missile facilities at the cost of a much larger crew.

segments.title: Estimating the SCX 26 concept's displacement
segments.body: Deck shape and overall proportions are the basis for comparing the two designs. The discussion puts a possible steel SCX 26 closer to 12,000 tonnes. It also considers a larger interpretation at 16,000 tonnes. These are estimates for hypothetical builds, while the 8,000-tonne figure refers to the concept ship.

evidence.note: The possible displacement of a steel SCX 26 is compared with the stated concept figure.
MEKO A400 comparison and discussion of larger displacement estimates.

segments.summary: The French SCX 26 is compared with the German MEKO A400 to explain why a steel version might exceed its 8,000-tonne concept figure.

segments.title: A fleet of Habakkuk carriers
segments.body: The thought experiment starts with several giant carriers available to the same fleet. They are imagined staying in service for decades. Those assumptions turn an engineering proposal for a single ship into a question about the size and service life of an entire carrier force.

evidence.note: The discussion imagines four or five ships on Project Habakkuk's scale entering service.

segments.summary: The discussion imagines four or five ships on Project Habakkuk's scale entering service.

segments.title: Age of Sail parallels for space commerce
segments.body: Regular peacetime convoys seem economically unlikely in this scenario. Merchant ships would operate individually where patrols and surveillance were sparse. International law could still apply, with enforcement depending on the forces actually present. That gap is the reason the merchants might provide for their own protection.

evidence.note: An Age of Sail analogy compares independent armed merchants with convoys and asks who would police a scattered trade network.

segments.summary: An Age of Sail analogy compares independent armed merchants with convoys and asks who would police a scattered trade network.
segments.question: Would future space travel resemble the Age of Sail, with independent armed merchant ships?
segments.answerShort: Independent armed merchants are plausible in the scenario because routine peacetime convoys would be costly and widely scattered trade would be hard to police.

segments.title: Reloading missile launchers on a Habakkuk-sized ship
segments.body: The reply focuses on how a crew would move stores around the ship and reach the launch area. A platform the size of Habakkuk might have dedicated storage and enough space for handling equipment. This is a modern extrapolation from the scale of the historical carrier proposal.

evidence.note: A hypothetical Habakkuk-sized carrier shows why onboard space matters for replenishing missiles at sea.

segments.summary: A hypothetical Habakkuk-sized carrier shows why onboard space matters for replenishing missiles at sea.
segments.question: How might a very large carrier accommodate reloadable missile launchers?
segments.answerShort: A ship on Habakkuk's scale could have enough room for separate storage and equipment to service its launchers at sea.

segments.title: Project Habakkuk alongside the Ford class
segments.body: The smaller Habakkuk figure discussed here is about 610 metres. A Ford-class carrier is put at about 337 metres. Even the smaller Habakkuk proposal is close to twice as long as this modern comparator. The estimate of up to a kilometre refers to a larger version.

evidence.note: A comparison with the Gerald R. Ford class puts the Habakkuk proposals in scale against a modern fleet carrier.

segments.summary: A comparison with the Gerald R. Ford class puts the Habakkuk proposals in scale against a modern fleet carrier.

segments.title: When steam displaced sail in the Royal Navy
segments.body: Steam offered a way to move when winds and tides would otherwise delay or constrain a ship. The Royal Navy fitted engines before it could count on them for every voyage. A sailing rig remained useful while machinery reliability improved. The 1880s and 1890s are given as the period when ships were consistently built without sailing masts.

evidence.note: Engine reliability determined how long ships kept their sailing rigs after the Royal Navy recognised the advantages of steam.

segments.summary: Engine reliability determined how long ships kept their sailing rigs after the Royal Navy recognised the advantages of steam.
segments.question: When did the Royal Navy recognise that steam would replace sail?
segments.answerShort: The advantage was clear early. It took decades for engines to become reliable enough for ships to dispense with sailing masts consistently.

segments.title: A Japanese answer to the British N3 battleships
segments.body: The question proposes a 20-inch-gunned Japanese battleship if Britain had built the N3 design. The reply places another procurement decision first, whether Japan would build the planned Number 13 class in the same scenario. The choice of gun size remains open.

evidence.note: The viewer asks about 20-inch guns and the answer points to Japan's own planned capital ships.

segments.summary: A counterfactual about British N3 construction asks whether Japan would have moved to 20-inch guns.
segments.question: Would Japan have pursued a 20-inch-gunned battleship if Britain had built the N3 class?
segments.answerShort: The reply envisages Japan first building its own more powerful planned battleships. It leaves any later move to 20-inch guns open.

segments.title: Testing Maximus against a Narvik force in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The trial uses a custom Maximus battleship and includes friendly destroyers screening it. The game separates the opposing destroyers into groups. As one group moves to help the other, the battleship engages it and sinks destroyers in succession. The game outcome depends on the separation of those forces. Near the end, the opposing force is down to one destroyer and the friendly destroyers are reported intact. The open-water setup is part of the explanation for that result.

evidence.note: Request to try the Maximus design against a force inspired by Narvik.
Trial with separate groups of destroyers and difficulties managing the screen.
One enemy destroyer is reported left and the friendly destroyers are reported intact.

segments.summary: A viewer request leads to a simulated battleship trial against destroyers in open water, inspired by Narvik.
segments.question: Can the Maximus design take on a destroyer force based on Narvik in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts?
segments.answerShort: In the open-water trial, Maximus defeats most of the opposing destroyers piecemeal as they try to regroup. The friendly destroyers are reported intact near the end.

segments.title: Why early boilers took time to adapt to ships
segments.body: Mining and railway boilers supplied early precedents for marine steam. Development on land was still underway as navies considered the technology for ships. Existing designs caused problems at sea that took time to identify and solve. The benefits of steam were apparent before the machinery could be relied on for naval service.

evidence.note: The Royal Navy's adoption of steam depended partly on adapting boilers developed for mining and railways.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy's adoption of steam depended partly on adapting boilers developed for mining and railways.

segments.title: Maximus and the displacement cost of armament
segments.body: The design removes casemate guns and calls for 4.5-inch secondary guns. The ship is still well over its displacement limit. Several armour changes save less weight than expected. With the main battery up to twelve guns, the game designer has to decide what protection and secondary weapons can fit around it.

evidence.note: The simulated Maximus battleship tests how much space and weight the main battery leaves for armour and secondary guns.

segments.summary: The simulated Maximus battleship tests how much space and weight the main battery leaves for armour and secondary guns.

segments.title: Why the game trial uses stock design rules
segments.body: The base game's rules determine the weight and balance constraints in the Maximus exercise. They give the design requests a common starting point. A mod could change the constraints and lead to a different result from the same brief.

evidence.note: The unmodified game provides a common reference for weight and balance in viewer-requested ship designs.

segments.summary: The unmodified game provides a common reference for weight and balance in viewer-requested ship designs.

segments.title: Maximus and the game's weight budget
segments.body: The designer looks at superstructure and main-deck protection and moves components to free space. Littorio provides a reference for the layout during the revisions. The game limits direct control over ballast calculations, even as it requires more changes to the fit. The model makes room for 4.5-inch secondary guns, though some planned mounts still cannot be placed.

evidence.note: Deck protection, ballast and gun placement complicate the effort to finish the model.

segments.summary: Deck protection, ballast and gun placement complicate the effort to finish the model.

segments.title: Controlling destroyer screens in the Narvik game trial
segments.body: One destroyer collides with the battleship it is meant to protect. The opposing destroyers become separated and have to pass the battleship to support the group under attack. Some friendly ships move out of the positions expected of them. Giving the destroyers different jobs keeps one close and sends another to hunt.

evidence.note: A Narvik-inspired simulation shows how a destroyer screen can lose its position and how separated ships can struggle to regroup.

segments.summary: A Narvik-inspired simulation shows how a destroyer screen can lose its position and how separated ships can struggle to regroup.

segments.title: Habakkuk as a floating airfield
segments.body: The proposal is to keep a large carrier off a shore position and use it as an airfield. A runway of about a kilometre could give many aircraft room to take off even when the platform was stationary. Feasibility would still depend on the aircraft and the conditions for take-off.

evidence.note: The response considers anchoring a carrier offshore and using a kilometre of runway without moving the ship.

segments.summary: A kilometre-long variant raises the possibility of operating aircraft from a stationary offshore runway.

segments.title: Habakkuk's proposed runway and pykrete construction
segments.body: Successively larger layouts are described at roughly 600 metres, a kilometre and around a mile. A longer runway brings different types of aircraft into consideration. Up to 18 knots is discussed as a projection for a moving design, which would allow more airflow over the deck. If pykrete worked on that scale, the same material could be considered for other large structures.

evidence.note: The discussion follows Habakkuk layouts from roughly 600 metres to a speculative mile-long deck.

segments.summary: The discussion follows Habakkuk layouts from roughly 600 metres to a speculative mile-long deck.

segments.title: What if HMS Hood had 20-inch guns?
segments.body: The ship editor needs a later technology setting to make the large guns available. The hull and fittings give the result the appearance of a modernisation. The game build uses oil-fired geared turbines and sacrifices some cruising range to cut weight. Armour can still help even when the ship cannot carry enough to resist its own main guns. The model comes out at about 50,000 tons with eight 20-inch guns.

evidence.note: A game rebuild of Hood shows what changes when eight 20-inch guns drive the choice of hull, armour and cruising range.

segments.summary: A game rebuild of Hood shows what changes when eight 20-inch guns drive the choice of hull, armour and cruising range.
segments.question: What would a version of HMS Hood armed with 20-inch guns look like?
segments.answerShort: The game rebuild produces a roughly 50,000-ton battlecruiser with eight 20-inch guns. The battery calls for later technology and compromises on cruising range and armour.

segments.title: Dazzle camouflage and interwar modern art
segments.body: Some modern artists were jokingly described as former dazzle painters who had run out of ships to work on. A naval camouflage pattern was still familiar enough in the interwar years for the comparison to work. The anecdote concerns the resemblance and the joke it inspired.

evidence.note: A joke from the 1920s and 1930s linked modern art to the painters who had once put dazzle patterns on ships.

segments.summary: A joke from the 1920s and 1930s linked modern art to the painters who had once put dazzle patterns on ships.

segments.title: An oversized British battlecruiser at the Washington Naval Conference
segments.body: The gaming scenario gives Britain a capital ship with unusually large guns and displacement. Those characteristics would make it difficult for the other powers to accept it as an exception. If Britain insisted on retaining the ship, the parties would need a substantially different settlement. The ship's military value is the political obstacle to a deal in this scenario.

evidence.note: A counterfactual asks whether Britain could keep an exceptionally large, heavily armed ship under the historical Washington settlement.

segments.summary: A counterfactual asks whether Britain could keep an exceptionally large, heavily armed ship under the historical Washington settlement.
segments.question: How would a much larger British battlecruiser affect the Washington Naval Treaty if Britain insisted on keeping it?
segments.answerShort: The treaty would be unlikely to follow its historical form. The other powers would have strong reasons to oppose Britain retaining a ship of that size and gun power on the same terms.

segments.title: Superfiring wing turrets in the Orion studies
segments.body: A British six-turret proposal is compared with contemporary German battleships that also carried six turrets. In this comparison, the British layout puts ten guns on a broadside and eight ahead or astern, against about eight and six respectively for the German layout. A centreline battery gives the Orions the desired broadside with less construction difficulty. Dropping the wing turrets allows a slimmer hull and simplifies protection for ammunition and hoists. Jack Fisher is named later as an advocate of wing turrets.

evidence.note: Question and comparison of British and German mount arrangements, gun arcs and shell-hoist protection.
Jack Fisher is identified as a supporter of wing turrets.

segments.summary: An Orion-class design study illustrates why the Royal Navy considered superfiring wing turrets and why it settled on a centreline battery.
segments.question: Did the Royal Navy consider battleships with superfiring wing turrets?
segments.answerShort: Yes. The arrangement was considered for the Orion class. Centreline turrets offered the desired broadside with fewer construction and protection complications.

segments.title: Triple turrets for the Orion class
segments.body: The alternative would adapt a Vickers triple turret under development and give Orion five triple 13.5-inch mountings. The proposed arrangement is credited with a fifteen-gun broadside and six guns bearing ahead or astern. A Queen Elizabeth class with twelve 15-inch guns is offered as a possible consequence in that counterfactual. The case for twins turns on operating speed, space and safety, as well as the complexity of triple mountings.

evidence.note: A five-turret alternative for Orion raises the question of how an early turn to triple mounts could have affected later British battleships.

segments.summary: A five-turret alternative for Orion raises the question of how an early turn to triple mounts could have affected later British battleships.

segments.title: Estimated range of a 20-inch/50 naval gun
segments.body: The calculation puts conventional range in the mid-50s of kilometres. A 16-inch/50 gun provides a comparison at roughly 39 to 40 km. The larger gun's reach would exceed a battleship's ability to acquire a target at that distance for much of the period under discussion, and a low rate of fire would also limit its utility. A barrel 50 calibres long at approximately 500 mm bore would be about 25 metres long. The calculation leaves shell weight open.

evidence.note: A rough range estimate for a hypothetical 20-inch gun leads into the limits of long-range naval gunnery.

segments.summary: A rough range estimate for a hypothetical 20-inch gun leads into the limits of long-range naval gunnery.
segments.question: How much range and throw weight might a 20-inch/50 gun provide?
segments.answerShort: The rough estimate is about 55 km. The discussion leaves shell weight open and points to target acquisition and rate of fire as limits on useful range.

segments.title: The 112,000-ton British battleship limit in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The battleship is the largest ship type available in this setup. The British figure comes from the hull selected in the designer. Limits for other nations are left as an estimate. The discussion treats about 1950 as the cutoff in the question and expects little difference in battleship options across the remaining game years.

evidence.note: A viewer asks how big a warship can get within a late-game cutoff. The British battleship designer shows a 112,000-ton cap.

segments.summary: A viewer asks how big a warship can get within a late-game cutoff. The British battleship designer shows a 112,000-ton cap.
segments.question: What is the largest, most heavily armed ship you can build within the game's late-period cutoff?
segments.answerShort: A battleship. The British hull shown has a 112,000-ton limit.

segments.title: Engines and propellant choices on a late-game battleship
segments.body: Poor engine efficiency prompts a look at the ship's fuel and propulsion choices. The heavy main battery also has a slow rate of fire. Cordite I is preferred for extending gun range. Among the available options, double-base propellant gives the best range bonus, reported as roughly 7.5 percent in the game.

evidence.note: A late-game battleship design runs into propulsion and gunnery constraints, including a preferred propellant unavailable for the build.

segments.summary: A late-game battleship design runs into propulsion and gunnery constraints, including a preferred propellant unavailable for the build.

segments.title: Where the weight goes in a 175,000-ton battleship design
segments.body: Engines, boilers, bulkheads, heavy turrets and upper armour are among the major entries in the breakdown. The build is about 175,000 tons before weight-saving changes begin. The large turrets are prominent among the items that can be reduced. The original gun count is one of the first choices to come under pressure.

evidence.note: A weight breakdown shows why the game battleship is far above its 112,000-ton hull cap.

segments.summary: A weight breakdown shows why the game battleship is far above its 112,000-ton hull cap.

segments.title: Triple versus quadruple turrets on a game battleship
segments.body: Triple turrets retain three-quarters of the original barrels and substantially reduce the battery's weight. The game's rate of fire, base accuracy and aiming speed all improve after the switch. The explanation is that three guns in a mounting are easier to operate than four. The number of barrels is only one measure of battery performance in the designer.

evidence.note: Switching from sixteen guns to twelve saves weight and improves several gunnery statistics.

segments.summary: Switching from sixteen guns to twelve saves weight and improves several gunnery statistics.

segments.title: Trading speed and endurance for battleship armour
segments.body: The turret change leaves further cuts to make. Changes to ammunition settings accompany a reduction in range to just under 11,000 on the game's readout and a drop in speed to 30 knots. The redesign leaves about 9,000 tons available for auxiliary machinery and revised armour. The next choices include a 16-inch main belt, a 4-inch inner belt and a 2-inch inner deck.

evidence.note: A 30-knot target and shorter operating range get an overweight game battleship under its cap and free weight for protection.

segments.summary: A 30-knot target and shorter operating range get an overweight game battleship under its cap and free weight for protection.

segments.title: How secondary guns affect engagement range in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The game's automated ships tend to close until their secondary guns can engage. This design has no secondary battery, and it fires from farther away. The opposing battleship appears to be in trouble after relatively few hits. The aim in this simulation is to make use of that initial range advantage.

evidence.note: A trial illustrates how removing the secondary battery can keep an automated battleship firing its main guns from farther away.

segments.summary: A trial illustrates how removing the secondary battery can keep an automated battleship firing its main guns from farther away.

segments.title: How replacing the Pensacolas could change US treaty cruiser design
segments.body: The premise is that a different heavy cruiser design replaces the Pensacola class around the time it enters service. Pensacola was the first American treaty cruiser class. In this scenario the US Navy would probably use the substitute as the basis for its next cruisers. The identity of the proposed replacement class is unclear.

evidence.note: A counterfactual asks which ships would provide the starting point for later US treaty cruisers.

segments.summary: A counterfactual asks which ships would provide the starting point for later US treaty cruisers.
segments.question: How might replacing the Pensacola class affect later US Navy treaty cruiser designs?
segments.answerShort: Later treaty cruisers would probably draw on the substitute heavy cruiser design.

segments.title: Would a 152 mm gun make a missile destroyer a cruiser?
segments.body: A cruiser in the design sense used here would require a more substantial redesign than a change in the main gun. Current destroyers and many frigates already carry out cruising and presence missions associated with cruisers. The duties can overlap even where the classifications differ.

evidence.note: A change in main-gun calibre raises a question about how ships are classed and what duties they perform.

segments.summary: A change in main-gun calibre raises a question about how ships are classed and what duties they perform.
segments.question: Would fitting a 152 mm gun to a guided-missile destroyer hull make it a cruiser?
segments.answerShort: A cruiser would require a more substantial design change, although many destroyers and frigates already undertake cruiser-like presence missions.

segments.title: How early could warships have carried missiles?
segments.body: The premise is that naval planners recognised the technology's potential early. The programme would have needed sustained funding, time and personnel. Under those assumptions, some form of shipboard capability is considered conceivable by World War II.

evidence.note: A speculative timeline begins with missile experiments in the early 1930s and considers what an early development programme could have delivered.

segments.summary: A speculative timeline begins with missile experiments in the early 1930s and considers what an early development programme could have delivered.
segments.question: How early could a navy conceivably have converted warships to carry missiles?
segments.answerShort: A programme backed heavily enough in the 1930s might have yielded some form of shipboard capability by World War II.

segments.title: British warship missile conversions compared with US practice
segments.body: Britain considered missile fits for existing ships and did some experimental work. Relatively few of the conversions implied by the question went ahead. British refits more often changed the missile equipment of ships that already carried missiles. The exchange gives a comparison with US practice at the level of programmes in general.

evidence.note: The question concerns early experiments and what usually happened when Britain changed the armament of existing ships.

segments.summary: The question concerns early experiments and what usually happened when Britain changed the armament of existing ships.
segments.question: Did Britain convert existing warships to carry missiles, or draw up plans to do so?
segments.answerShort: Britain explored conversions and carried out relatively few. Refits more commonly involved ships that already carried missiles.

segments.title: Destroyer screening and specialist frigates
segments.body: Anti-submarine warfare is one element of screening a force. A destroyer's screening remit can also include air defence. Frigates may specialise in anti-submarine warfare or be designed around other duties. The job assigned within a fleet helps explain the distinction in this account.

evidence.note: A destroyer's fleet-screening remit is compared with the specialist tasks often assigned to frigates.

segments.summary: A destroyer's fleet-screening remit is compared with the specialist tasks often assigned to frigates.

segments.title: Could Norwegian vessels cover a British replacement requirement?
segments.body: The suggestion concerns the government's possible expectations for a purchase from Norway. A timetable for a dedicated replacement is left open. The ageing British vessel is difficult to identify in the question.

evidence.note: Unclear ship name in the question, followed by speculation about ships bought from Norway.

segments.summary: The reply to a question about an ageing British ship suggests the government may be counting on vessels it is buying from Norway.
segments.question: When might the British government act on the need to replace the ageing vessel discussed here?
segments.answerShort: The government may be hoping vessels it is buying from Norway will cover the role.
